title: Jaishankar Urges Urgent Multilateral Reform Through Stronger Minilateralism
excerpt: At the Raisina Dialogue in Abu Dhabi, India's foreign minister cited a decade of India-UAE partnership as the model for smaller-group cooperation in a changing global order.
body:
• External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar told the Raisina Dialogue's Middle East session in Abu Dhabi that reform of multilateralism is urgent and can be supported through stronger minilateralism — cooperation among smaller groups of countries.
  • He cited the India-UAE partnership of the last decade as a model of two nations responding to a changing global order.
  • Jaishankar held bilateral talks with UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al-Nahyan under the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
  • For the roughly 4.3 million Indians living in the UAE — about 35 percent of its population — the partnership underpins trade, energy and consular ties that shape daily life in the Gulf.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar on Wednesday called for urgent reform of multilateral institutions, arguing that stronger cooperation among smaller groups of countries — minilateralism — can support a system struggling to reach consensus. He made the remarks in Abu Dhabi at a session of the Middle East edition of the Raisina Dialogue titled "The World Ahead: Power, Purpose & Possibility," alongside UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al-Nahyan, according to India Today.

"The reform of multilateralism is urgent. It can be supported through stronger minilateralism."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister of India

Change, shocks and new partnerships

Jaishankar said the pace of change in the global order is increasing, driven by both long-term trends and immediate shocks, and that countries respond according to their specific situations. "New partnerships and fresh options are inevitably explored in that pursuit," he said in a post on X after the discussion, reported by IANS via hi INDiA. That response, he added, requires going beyond traditional comfort zones and developing sharper strategic awareness.

https://x.com/DrSJaishankar/status/2110452974023745661

Minilateralism refers to cooperation among a relatively small group of countries on specific issues. Such groupings can move faster than broad multilateral forums, and India has leaned on them increasingly — in the Quad, in trilateral formats with Gulf and European partners, and in issue-based coalitions on energy, technology and connectivity.

India-UAE as the example

Jaishankar pointed to his hosts as the proof of concept. "The India-UAE partnership of the last decade is a great example of our two nations responding to the changing global environment," he said. He separately described his bilateral meeting with Sheikh Abdullah as "a warm and productive meeting," in which the two exchanged perspectives on bilateral and global issues in the spirit of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=lLp52S4vr_s

The framework is substantial. The Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, in force since May 2022, structures bilateral trade and investment, and cooperation has expanded across energy, defence, security and technology. The visit, during a three-day official trip, was also a review of that progress, and Jaishankar met Georgia's foreign minister Maka Botchorishvili on the sidelines.

A tense regional backdrop

The diplomacy played out against regional strain, including conflict involving Iran and a sharp escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen. The Indian consulate in Dubai said on Sunday that 22 Indian crew members were rescued from the crude oil tanker MT Gem No. 2 after an accident off the Ras Al Khaimah coast, and that all were safe — a reminder of how directly Gulf instability touches Indian nationals.

What it means for Indians in the Gulf

Indians are the UAE's largest ethnic community, estimated at 4.3 million in 2024 and about 35 percent of the population, with Kerala the largest state of origin. For that diaspora, the partnership Jaishankar praised is not abstract: it governs energy security, remittance corridors, consular protection and the business environment in which Indian firms operate across the Emirates. Stronger minilateral formats, in New Delhi's telling, are how countries of India's and the UAE's size keep that practical cooperation moving when larger institutions stall.
